# Profiling Python: Measure First, With cProfile, timeit, tracemalloc and py-spy

Last verified: 2026-10-28 against docs.python.org/3.14 (profile), docs.python.org/3 (timeit, tracemalloc, cmdline), the py-spy README and py-spy 0.4.2 help, and Python 3.14.3 run on macOS. All demos rerun; py-spy dump could not run without root.

Starts from: lesson 05-python-for-programmers (functions, `uv run`) and lesson 01-asyncio-concurrency (what blocks a loop). *Profiling* means measuring where a program spends its time or memory. This lesson quotes no speed figures from memory; every number below was captured on one Mac (an Apple M4 laptop), and each has the command that produced it. That Mac reported macOS Low Power Mode on (`pmset -g`) during the fact-check rerun, and every time here came out about 2 to 2.5 times what an earlier drafting run recorded (the same cProfile command: 0.275 s then, 0.574 s now; `sum(xs)` in Demo 3: 177 usec then, 436 usec now). Low Power Mode is the likely cause; I could not switch it off to test that. The ratios between the numbers stayed about the same. That is why you name the hardware and its state: times compare only on one machine in one state.

## The problem and why it matters

"The service is slow" is a feeling. A fix aimed at a feeling usually changes the wrong thing: you tune the model call and the time was in string handling around it. A profiler turns the feeling into a list: which functions, how many calls, how much time.

In glue code the usual suspects are boring: work done per item that should be done per batch, strings built character by character, caches that never shrink, imports at startup, and serialisation (turning objects into bytes and back) around a model call. Measure in this order: *is it slow, where, did my change fix it*.

## First principles

1. **Measure before you change anything.** Guessing loses to a tool. Edit one thing, re-measure, keep it only if the measurement improved.
2. **Wall time versus CPU time.** *Wall time* is the clock on the wall: how long you waited. *CPU time* is time a processor spent running your code. Waiting on a network adds wall time and no CPU time.
3. **A deterministic profiler** records every function call and return, so it knows exact call counts. The docs say it monitors "all function call, function return, and exception events". It slows the program while it watches. `cProfile` is the standard one.
4. **A sampling (statistical) profiler** looks at the program every few milliseconds and records what it is doing, "deduc[ing] where time is being spent". It has low overhead and gives relative shares, not exact counts. `py-spy` is one; its `record` command samples 100 times a second by default (`py-spy record --help`).
5. **Benchmarks are noisy.** The `timeit` docs advise taking the `min()` of several repeats, because slower runs are "typically not caused by variability in Python's speed, but by other processes interfering".
6. **A profile shows shares, not wrongness.** The top function is where to look, if its share is big enough to matter.

## How it works

### The loop

```
   "it is slow"
        |
        v
  reproduce it with a timer on a small input
  that has the real shape of the data
        |
        v
  profile: which function has the top share?
        |
        v
  change ONE thing; check the answer is the same
        |
        v
  re-time without the profiler
        |
        +--> faster? keep it. Not faster? revert.
```

### Deterministic versus sampling

```
  cProfile (every event)         py-spy (every few ms)

  call f  --> note time          ...tick: stack is a>b>f
  call g  --> note time          ...tick: stack is a>b>f
  ret  g  --> note time          ...tick: stack is a>c
  ret  f  --> note time
  exact counts, adds overhead    no code changes, no
  inside the process             restart; sees a live
                                 process from outside
```

### Demo 1: find the hot spot with cProfile

`pipeline.py` normalises text (keeps letters, digits and spaces, lower-cases) and checksums it, once for each of 2,000 requests. `normalize` builds its result character by character.

```python
def normalize(text):
    out = ""
    for ch in text:
        if ch.isalnum() or ch == " ":
            out += ch.lower()
    return out

def checksum(s):
    return sum(s.encode()) % 65521

def handle(text):
    return checksum(normalize(text))

def main():
    texts = ["Hello, World! " * 50 for _ in range(2000)]
    return sum(handle(t) for t in texts)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(main())
```

Run `uv run python -m cProfile -s tottime pipeline.py`. Captured here on macOS (Apple M4, Python 3.14.3, Low Power Mode), selected rows (the program's own output, `114800000`, prints first):

```text
2612007 function calls (2610007 primitive calls) in 0.574 seconds

   ncalls  tottime  percall  cumtime  percall filename:lineno(function)
     2000    0.346    0.000    0.568    0.000 pipeline.py:1(normalize)
  1400000    0.119    0.000    0.119    0.000 {method 'isalnum' of 'str' objects}
  1200000    0.103    0.000    0.103    0.000 {method 'lower' of 'str' objects}
     2000    0.001    0.000    0.005    0.000 pipeline.py:8(checksum)
```

Read the columns: `ncalls` is the number of calls (the docs: when it shows two numbers like `3/1`, the function recursed, total calls first and primitive calls second); `tottime` is time inside the function itself, excluding what it calls; `cumtime` is time including everything it calls. `normalize` dominates both, and `checksum` is nearly free. Save the data with `-o out.prof` and explore it with `pstats.Stats('out.prof').strip_dirs().sort_stats('cumulative').print_stats(5)`.

### Demo 2: fix it, prove the same answer, re-time

```python
import cProfile, re, timeit
import pipeline

_JUNK = re.compile(r"[^A-Za-z0-9 ]")
def normalize_fast(text):
    return _JUNK.sub("", text).lower()

t = "Hello, World! " * 50
assert pipeline.normalize(t) == normalize_fast(t)       # same answer first

old = min(timeit.repeat(lambda: pipeline.normalize(t), number=2000, repeat=5))
new = min(timeit.repeat(lambda: normalize_fast(t), number=2000, repeat=5))
print(f"old normalize x2000: best of 5 = {old:.3f}s")
print(f"new normalize x2000: best of 5 = {new:.3f}s")

plain = min(timeit.repeat(pipeline.main, number=1, repeat=5))
def profiled():
    with cProfile.Profile():
        pipeline.main()
under = min(timeit.repeat(profiled, number=1, repeat=5))
print(f"main() plain {plain:.3f}s, under cProfile {under:.3f}s")
```

Captured here on macOS (Low Power Mode; three reruns agreed to within 0.006 s):

```text
old normalize x2000: best of 5 = 0.099s
new normalize x2000: best of 5 = 0.030s
main() plain 0.103s, under cProfile 0.567s
```

Two lessons. The rewrite was faster here, and we kept it only because the assertion proved the same output on this input (ASCII only, so a real fix needs more tests). And the profiler made `main()` several times slower, so cProfile's *absolute times* are inflated; use it for ranking and call counts, then confirm with an unprofiled timer.

### Demo 3: command-line timing, and what native code changes

```bash
uv run python -m timeit -s "xs=list(range(100000))" "sum(xs)"
uv run python -m timeit -s "xs=list(range(100000))" "t=0
for x in xs: t+=x"
uv run --with numpy python -m timeit \
  -s "import numpy as np; xs=np.arange(100000)" "xs.sum()"
```

Captured here on macOS (Low Power Mode; `timeit` picks the loop count itself):

```text
500 loops, best of 5: 436 usec per loop
100 loops, best of 5: 2.44 msec per loop
20000 loops, best of 5: 14.4 usec per loop
```

The same sum over 100,000 integers: a Python `for` loop, the built-in `sum` (a C function), and NumPy (a numeric library whose arrays are processed by compiled code). One machine, one size: rerun on yours.

Type hints are not a speed tool: `timeit` of `add(a, b)` with and without hints gave 0.049 to 0.054 s per million calls in four interleaved runs here, with no pattern between the two. Hints help checkers, not the interpreter.

### Demo 4: find a memory leak with tracemalloc

`tracemalloc` is a standard-library tool that records where Python allocated memory. A cache with no limit, fed 20,000 distinct keys, against `functools.lru_cache(maxsize=100)` (an *LRU* cache evicts the least recently used entry):

```python
import functools, tracemalloc
cache = {}
def lookup_unbounded(key):
    if key not in cache:
        cache[key] = f"{key}" * 200
    return cache[key]

@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=100)
def lookup_bounded(key):
    return f"{key}" * 200

cases = [("unbounded dict", lookup_unbounded), ("lru_cache(100)", lookup_bounded)]
for name, fn in cases:
    tracemalloc.start()
    s1 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
    for i in range(20_000):
        fn(i)
    s2 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
    cur, peak = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
    top = s2.compare_to(s1, "lineno")[0]
    print(f"{name:15} traced now {cur/1e6:6.2f} MB | top line {top.traceback[0].lineno}")
    tracemalloc.stop()
```

Captured here on macOS:

```text
unbounded dict  traced now  19.82 MB | top line 5
lru_cache(100)  traced now   0.12 MB | top line 10
```

`compare_to` between two snapshots names the allocating line (the docs sort the result by the absolute size difference; `traceback[0]` is the allocation site only because `tracemalloc.start()` keeps one frame by default). Tracing slows the program (about 5 times on a small allocation loop here: 0.042 s plain, 0.209 s traced; the docs give no figure), so use it in a test or staging run.

### Demo 5: import time, and a sampler that was not run

```bash
uv run python -X importtime -c "import asyncio" 2> imp.txt; tail -3 imp.txt
```

Captured here on macOS (Low Power Mode; microseconds: self, then cumulative, as the header line `import time: self [us] | cumulative | imported package` says; the last line is the outermost import):

```text
import time:       429 |        429 |     asyncio.selector_events
import time:       435 |       1089 |   asyncio.unix_events
import time:       235 |      42201 | asyncio
```

Four runs gave 41,666 to 44,007 us for `asyncio` here, and an earlier drafting run gave 16,640 to 28,751 us, so repeat it before believing one figure. The docs add that the output may be broken in multi-threaded programs. It is a one-time startup cost; this flag shows which imports are heavy.

**Not run here:** `py-spy`. It is installed (0.4.2), but on macOS it must run as root, and this session does not use `sudo`. Its README documents `py-spy dump --pid PID` (print the call stack of each Python thread), `py-spy top --pid PID` (live view) and `py-spy record -o profile.svg --pid PID` (flame graph, a chart where wide boxes are where time goes). On Linux the README says the default is to require root when attaching to a process that is not a child, which the `ptrace_scope` sysctl can relax; for Docker it says to start the container with `--cap-add SYS_PTRACE`. Those Linux and Docker steps were not run here. The README says "OSX always requires running as root". The attempt here printed `This program requires root on OSX.`

## Worked failure scenario

**Symptom:** an embedding gateway's p99 latency (the time that 99% of requests beat; only the slowest 1% take longer) doubled after a release. Model-server logs show the same time per call.

1. **Reproduce.** Replay a recorded batch of real requests through the handler function alone, timed with `perf_counter`, best of several runs. If this does not show the slowdown, the problem is outside the function (queueing, a blocked loop; see 01).
2. **Rank.** Run the replay under `python -m cProfile -s tottime` and compare with the previous release's profile. A new top function, or a call count that jumped, is the lead.
3. **On the live service,** use a sampler (`py-spy dump` a few times; `record` for a flame graph) because you cannot restart it or accept cProfile's slowdown.
4. **Change one thing,** assert identical output, re-time.
5. **Memory growth** (resident memory, the RAM the process holds, rising over hours): take two `tracemalloc` snapshots an hour apart in staging and diff them.

**Fix and guard:** keep the replay as a benchmark script in the repo, report times with the hardware named, and never compare timings across machines.

## Tradeoffs

| Use when | Avoid when |
|---|---|
| cProfile on a reproducible script: exact call counts | Absolute times from a profiled run: overhead inflates them |
| A sampler (py-spy) on a live process | You cannot get root or ptrace permission; use cProfile in staging |
| `timeit` best-of-N for a small function | Timing I/O-heavy code; replay end to end |
| tracemalloc diffs for leaks | Always-on production tracing |

## Interview questions

1. Deterministic versus sampling profilers? *Probe:* which gives exact call counts? *Outline:* cProfile records every event, exact counts, more overhead; samplers look periodically, low overhead, shares only.
2. What do `tottime` and `cumtime` mean? *Outline:* self time versus including callees; look at `tottime` for the hot function, `cumtime` for the hot subtree.
3. How do you trust a fix that made the profile look faster? *Outline:* re-time unprofiled, assert same output, repeat, name the hardware.
4. The service leaks memory slowly. Steps? *Outline:* tracemalloc snapshots diffed; look for unbounded dicts, lists and caches; bound them.
5. How do you profile a process you cannot restart? *Outline:* py-spy by PID; needs root on macOS, extra permissions in containers.
6. Do type hints make code faster? *Outline:* not measured to; checkers use them.

**Whiteboard exercise:** a handler takes 40 ms per request and a replay shows 30 of it is "inside the handler". Lay out, in order, the commands you run, what each result would change in your plan, and when you stop.

## Checklist

1. I can say what wall time, CPU time and a profiler are.
2. I ran cProfile on `pipeline.py` and can name the hot function and why.
3. I can read `ncalls`, `tottime` and `cumtime`.
4. I know cProfile inflates absolute time (measured here).
5. I know what py-spy does and that I have not run it.

## Common wrong answers

- "Leave cProfile on in production." Its overhead was several times here.
- "The top function is always the problem." Only if its share is large and it is called more than needed.
- "Quote the profiled seconds as the speed." Re-time without the profiler.

## Sources

Checked on 2026-10-28:
- https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/profile.html: deterministic versus statistical profiling wording, `cProfile` command line (`-o`, `-s`, `-m`), column meanings, `primitive calls` and the `3/1` notation, `cProfile.Profile` as a context manager (3.8), `pstats` methods. The unversioned `/3/` page now serves the 3.15 documentation, where `cProfile` is an alias of `profiling.tracing` and a `profiling.sampling` module exists; Python 3.14.3 has no `profiling` package (`import profiling` raises `ModuleNotFoundError`).
- https://docs.python.org/3/library/tracemalloc.html: `start`, `take_snapshot`, `compare_to` (sorted by absolute size difference), `get_traced_memory` returns `(current, peak)`, frame order in a traceback, default of one frame. The page gives no slowdown figure; the roughly 5 times above is our own measurement.
- https://docs.python.org/3/library/timeit.html: `min()` of repeats and the "other processes interfering" wording, `perf_counter` default timer, command-line output format and automatic loop count, `repeat` default 5.
- https://docs.python.org/3/using/cmdline.html: `-X importtime` (module name, cumulative and self time; output may be broken in multi-threaded programs; the page does not state units or stderr, so those come from the captured header line and my `2>` redirect).
- https://github.com/benfred/py-spy (README) and `py-spy --help` / `py-spy record --help` (0.4.2): sampling profiler that needs no restart or code change, `dump`/`top`/`record` and `--pid`, 100 samples per second default, "OSX always requires running as root", Linux root-unless-child default and `ptrace_scope`, Docker `--cap-add SYS_PTRACE`.

Not run: py-spy sampling (needs root on macOS; only the root-required message was reproduced), any Linux profiler, `profiling.sampling` (3.15 only). All numbers are runs on one Apple M4 Mac, Python 3.14.3, in Low Power Mode, numpy as installed by `uv run --with`; rerun them on your machine.
